findings: B “… ett svepskäl som döljer ett annat motstånd” — refuted by «Ett svepskäl är det inte. Kostnaden är verklig och ska räknas med.»: the writer says in terms that it is not a pretext and that the cost is real.

C “utökas i den takt som ensemblen vänjer sig” — refuted by «Fler särskilda kvällar begär jag inte.» and «Att ensemblen vänjer sig vid remsan kan jag inte lova.»: she asks for no further special evenings at all and refuses to promise the ensemble will get used to it.

D “En skärm bör hänga ovanför lilla scenen också” — refuted by «Om lilla scenen kan bära samma sak vet jag inte.» and «något förslag för den scenen har jag inte»: she withholds judgement on the small stage and puts forward no proposal for it.
justification: Key A is stated as the writer's demand in «Från och med nästa spelår bör texten gå på varje föreställning på stora scenen, inte på fyra utvalda.», with the concession about the acting carried by «Ett svepskäl är det inte. Kostnaden är verklig och ska räknas med.» and «Ändå ska den bäras.».

findings: A “Den är märkt med slingans symbol” — refuted by «Slingans symbol finns längst ned på varje uppslag i programbladet och har gjort det i alla år.»: the loop symbol has its own fixed place at the foot of every spread, and it marks the hearing loop, a service the text separates from the text screen.

B “Den upprepas längst ned på varje uppslag” — refuted by «Slingans symbol finns längst ned på varje uppslag i programbladet och har gjort det i alla år.»: what recurs at the foot of every spread is the symbol; the row itself is the single wedged-in line of «har de textade föreställningarna en egen rad, inklämd mellan syntolkning och skolföreställningar».

C “Den anger vem som sköter tekniken” — refuted by «Längre bak i programbladet står Ingegerd Hörnfeldt under rubriken Text och teknik.»: the named technician stands further back in the programme under her own heading, not on that row.
justification: Key D restates %s. All three distractors take a true programme-layout detail and attach it to the wrong element, and each is displaced by a span that fixes where that detail actually sits.

findings: B “Hovarna klarade sig med broddar” — refuted by «En hov samlar hela djurets tyngd på en yta stor som en tallrik, och mot det hjälper varken broddar eller lättare lass.»: neither studs nor a lighter load helped against the load per hoof.
C “Hästarna drog kälken i stället” — refuted by «Lassen gick på kälke i stället, och kälken drogs för hand.» and «Hästen fick stå i stallet.»: the sledge was drawn by hand and the horse stayed in.
D “Hästarna användes till annat under de veckorna” — refuted by «Hästen fick stå i stallet.»: standing in the stable is the positive contrary of being put to other work in that period.
justification: Key A is a near-literal restatement of «Skaren som bar en karl gick sönder under hoven», and the hoof-loading sentence «En hov samlar hela djurets tyngd på en yta stor som en tallrik, och mot det hjälper varken broddar eller lättare lass.» makes it the only option consistent with the passage.

findings: A “Hushållen turades om och delade på vändorna” — refuted by «Var gård körde för sig, och sällan väntade någon in grannen.»: each farm drove for itself and rarely waited for a neighbour.

C “Barnen fick lasta medan de vuxna var ute och körde” — NOT refuted on a span. The only sentence in the text that mentions children is «Barnen provar den med hälen som vi gjorde, utan att det ska bli någon färd.», and it sits in the closing present-day frame opened by «Nu plogas vägarna, och maskinerna tar sig fram i lös snö.»: it describes today's children playing, and says nothing about who loaded when the crust was worked. The nearest contrary is inferential only (the heel test is the thing done “innan man ger sig ut”, and “som vi gjorde” puts the child narrator among those who went out) — a division of labour the text never states, i.e. unsupported rather than refuted.

D “Man fortsatte tills sista lasset var hemma” — refuted by «Ett lass som inte är hemma vid tio blir liggande till nästa natt.», read with «Bärigheten varar några timmar. Man ger sig i väg vid fyra, i mörker, och vid tio är det över.»: the bearing ends at ten whatever is still out, and a load not home by then is abandoned until the next night.
justification: Flag, not kill: key B is well supported by «Man såg på himlen och bestämde sig kvällen innan.» and «Veckorna kom när de kom.», and A and D die hard on spans, but rebuilt option C is merely unsupported — nothing in the passage refutes children loading while the adults drove. C is not defensible as an answer to “vad framgår av texten”, so the item is not broken, but it does not meet this round's span-refutation bar and should be rebuilt against a sentence about who did the work.

findings: A “drove the cone through to the bottom of the bed at each point” — refuted by «how deep the cone sinks on the first blow, and how many blows take it to a hundred millimetres» against «The floor is 130 millimetres of washed silica sand, mixed through with chopped fibre and coated in wax, laid over a membrane and crushed stone.»: the count is defined to a hundred millimetres and the bed is 130.

B “let fall by hand, from whatever height each point seemed to need” — refuted by «a steel cone on a rod, under a ring weight raised to a collar and let fall»: the ring weight is raised to a collar, i.e. to a fixed drop.

D “spread between one arena and the next is wider than the spread between his two visits” — refuted by «The gap between my February morning and my July afternoon is still wider than the gap between this school and any other school I test.»: Pallenmoor states the comparison the other way round.
justification: Key C paraphrases «in the cold the first blow took the cone two-thirds as deep, and the count nearly doubled» exactly (shallower first blow, higher count), and the two readings are the two figures the instrument yields «how deep the cone sinks on the first blow, and how many blows take it to a hundred millimetres».

findings: A “wax had worn off the grains in the lower part of the bed” — refuted by «The sand itself had hardly changed: the grains he sieved came out much as the original specification had them, and the wax he brought up from the bottom was in better condition than the wax at the top.»: the wax from the bottom was in better condition than the wax at the top.

B “sand had broken down into finer grains than the specification called for” — refuted by the same span «The sand itself had hardly changed: the grains he sieved came out much as the original specification had them, and the wax he brought up from the bottom was in better condition than the wax at the top.»: the sieved grains came out much as specified.

C “Below the tines the bed had stayed loose, out of reach of the hoofprints above it” — refuted by «Eighty millimetres of it had not been turned since the day it was laid, and under nine years of hoofprints it had gone firm enough to lean a spade on.»: the unturned eighty millimetres had gone firm under nine years of hoofprints, the exact opposite on both halves of the claim.
justification: Key D is the fibre gradient stated in «In the top 50 millimetres the fibre came out at about 8 per cent by weight; lower down it was nearer 3.» (about 8 per cent above, nearer 3 below), found by the coring described in «Pallenmoor cored the bed in eleven places.».

findings: A “They went down more recently…” — refuted by «He has the same pair of grids from a hundred and forty other arenas, some of them older than this one.» and «The waxed ones move, whatever their age.»: some of the other arenas are older than this one, and the waxed ones move whatever their age.

C “A membrane under them holds the water in…” — refuted by «The floor is 130 millimetres of washed silica sand, mixed through with chopped fibre and coated in wax, laid over a membrane and crushed stone.»: the membrane is part of how THIS school is built, and this is the school that moves, so a membrane cannot be what keeps the sprinkler schools steady; the text attributes their damp to the sprinkler, never water retention to a membrane.

D “They are read at a different hour…” — refuted by «He has the same pair of grids from a hundred and forty other arenas, some of them older than this one.» against «He read a grid of thirty points at seven, with the school at three degrees, and the same grid at four, with it at eighteen.»: the same pair of grids, on the same seven-and-four protocol, is what he has from every arena.
justification: Key B is carried by the contrast in «In the schools laid on plain sand and fibre and kept damp with a sprinkler, the morning grid and the afternoon grid sit almost on top of one another.» and «The waxed ones move, whatever their age.»: plain sand and fibre stay put, waxed beds move regardless of age, so the absence of wax is the operative difference — and the wax mechanism in «Below about six degrees the coating is stiff, the grains lock together, and a hoof breaks the surface.» and «Above about twenty-five it goes slack, the grains slide past one another, and the floor gets deep.» supplies the reason. Rebuilt option C does not become a second defensible answer: the membrane is a feature the moving school shares.

findings: B “reads what the yard has since done as an answer to the soundness question” — refuted by «The tester measures a surface; there is no horse above the cone.» and «The yard has changed one thing and left the other alone.»: the writer brackets soundness as something the cone cannot reach, and reports the yard's response as half done, with the heaters costed and not ordered «Heaters have been costed and not ordered: the quote came to more than a month of winter lessons.».

C “treats the riders’ account as the thing the readings were brought in to correct” — refuted by «For two winters the riders here have been saying that the school changes under them: hard and slippery for a January lesson, deep and tiring by a July afternoon.» against «The yard has blamed the machine, then the mix, then the man on the tractor.» and «Then there is the machine, though not in the way the yard had blamed it.»: the readings bear the riders out; what they correct is the yard's blaming.

D “rates the trade’s brochures the fuller answer…” — refuted by «That is a good deal less than the trade’s brochures offer, and it is worth more than they are.»: the writer's valuation is the closing clause, that the careful, limited answer is worth more than the brochures.
justification: Key A restates «Here Pallenmoor is careful, and the care is the most useful thing about him.», reinforced by the same closing sentence. Noted: D's descriptive half is conceded by the text (the brochures do offer more), so the kill rests entirely on the evaluative sense of “rates” plus “it is worth more than they are” — the thinnest refutation in this unit, though it holds because the stem asks for the writer's position.

findings: A “the grains are probably freezing to one another” — refuted by «Below about six degrees the coating is stiff, the grains lock together, and a hoof breaks the surface.»: the cold-weather mechanism the text gives is a stiff paraffin coating locking the grains, and the cold reading was three degrees «He read a grid of thirty points at seven, with the school at three degrees, and the same grid at four, with it at eighteen.», above freezing.

B “A school that is kept warm will ride in February much as it rides in July” — refuted by «Above about twenty-five it goes slack, the grains slide past one another, and the floor gets deep.»: heating addresses only the below-six regime; the July fault is the above-twenty-five regime, which heating does not touch, and «I can’t put a number on it; these readings won’t carry one, and the blend on the grains changes from one supplier to the next.» refuses exactly this kind of quantified extrapolation.

D “The tractor’s work may matter more to the school than the temperature does” — refuted by «The temperature is doing more in that room than the tractor is»: the text's own ranking is the reverse, and the hedge “may” does not survive an explicit comparative.
justification: Key C names the two causes the text establishes: temperature through the wax «Below about six degrees the coating is stiff, the grains lock together, and a hoof breaks the surface.» «Above about twenty-five it goes slack, the grains slide past one another, and the floor gets deep.», and tine depth through «The leveller’s tines were set to 50 millimetres. The bed is 130.» and «Eighty millimetres of it had not been turned since the day it was laid, and under nine years of hoofprints it had gone firm enough to lean a spade on.». Both matter, with temperature ranked higher «The temperature is doing more in that room than the tractor is», which is what C asserts and D denies.

findings: A “Hence” — refuted by «the ending is unanimous: five seconds later the sound stops, and again there has been no signal»: the unanimous ending is presented as a second, parallel marvel (“again there has been no signal”), not as a consequence of the unanimous start, and «Ending is the harder half.» denies that it follows from it.

B “Rather” — refuted by «the ending is unanimous: five seconds later the sound stops, and again there has been no signal»: the clause adds a like case rather than correcting the preceding one; “again” signals sameness, which is incompatible with a corrective.

D “Elsewhere” — refuted by «the ending is unanimous: five seconds later the sound stops, and again there has been no signal»: the sentence stays in the same hall and moves five seconds forward in time, so a locative shift has nothing to attach to.
justification: Key C “Equally” is the parallel-case connective the frame requires, linking «and yet two hundred people find the same half-second.» to «the ending is unanimous: five seconds later the sound stops, and again there has been no signal».

findings: B “cut” — refuted by «The risk of putting your hands together in a quiet room is that the room may not» and «That is why the second pair of hands matters more than the first: it turns a private view into a public event.»: what is at risk is the room failing to follow, not anyone interrupting; “cut in” supplies the wrong event.

C “fall” — refuted by the frame «The risk of putting your hands together in a quiet room is that the room may not»: “fall in” means to take one's place in line, and the agreement sense needs “fall in with”, which the frame does not offer.

D “break” — refuted by «for the length of one clap you are alone with an opinion nobody asked for»: “break in” is an intrusion into something already running, but nothing is running — the clapper is alone.
justification: Key A “join in” is the action «That is why the second pair of hands matters more than the first: it turns a private view into a public event.» names: the second pair of hands turning a private view into a public event.

findings: A “transaction” — refuted by «about how long is decent, conducted at speed and without words»: the frame requires a process that is “about” a question of degree; a transaction is an exchange of value and does not take “about” in this sense.

C “bargain” — refuted by «about how long is decent, conducted at speed and without words» and «the sound comes down faster than it went up, and the coming-down is a»: a bargain is the outcome struck, not something “conducted”, and the gap is filled by the coming-down itself, which is the process under way.

D “settlement” — refuted by «about how long is decent, conducted at speed and without words» and «the sound comes down faster than it went up, and the coming-down is a»: a settlement is likewise the result reached, while the frame names the arriving-at, conducted at speed.
justification: Key B is the only process noun that takes both “about how long is decent” and “conducted”; C is the closest competitor and dies on “conducted”.

findings: A “rehearsed” — refuted by «No one has agreed to anything, there is no conductor to watch»: the text's whole point is that nothing about this is agreed or led.

B “outspoken” — refuted by the frame «Although what a hall gives an eight-year-old is»: the subject is what a hall gives, a sound of a certain warmth and length, and “outspoken” predicates of persons and opinions, not of applause.

C “brief” — refuted by «it is not permitted to run long. Four or five seconds, then a ragged tail»: “Although … is brief, it is not permitted to run long” is not a concession but a restatement, so the Although-frame itself kills it.
justification: Key D “wholehearted” is the only filler that makes «Although what a hall gives an eight-year-old is» a genuine concession against «it is not permitted to run long. Four or five seconds, then a ragged tail», and it matches the warmth the piece contrasts with the dutiful clap.

findings: A “narrowly” — refuted by the frame «A room asked for a big hand for a stranger will give one»: the adverb must characterise the manner of the giving, and “give one narrowly” does not read as a manner at all.

C “instinctively” — refuted by «A room asked for a big hand for a stranger will give one» and «and everybody present can hear that it is not the same sound the recorder player got»: the applause is given because it was asked for, and the hall can hear that it is not the spontaneous sound.

D “eagerly” — refuted by «and everybody present can hear that it is not the same sound the recorder player got»: eager applause would be the same sound the recorder player got, and the text says it audibly is not.
justification: Key B “dutifully” is what «and everybody present can hear that it is not the same sound the recorder player got» requires: a hall discharging a request, audibly unlike the sound given freely.

findings: B “spotted by its colour before it leaves the ward” — refuted by «Nothing shows on the ward; the colour comes with the spinning.»: nothing shows on the ward and the colour appears only after spinning.
C “Samples for blood gases go by tube…” — refuted by «Blood gases have never gone by tube; a porter walks those down.»: they have never gone by tube; a porter walks them.

D “rejected samples fell once the loop was slowed down” — refuted by «The loop runs at the speed it always has. Two bins are lined with foam, and rejects are down by about half.»: the loop runs at the speed it always has, and the halving follows the foam lining.
justification: Key A is Ashvenor's own attributed claim in «It’s the stop at the far end that does it», set up by «Between stations the shocks were tiny.», which is what the stem asks for.

findings: A “answered the claim without bringing the railway company’s plan into the letters” — refuted by «The neighbour’s attorney enclosed a tracing of the railway company’s deposited plan.»: the neighbour's attorney enclosed a tracing of that very plan.

B “the thorn on the bank had been left untended” — refuted by «cut from above by one and cleaned from below by the other, and had stood since the enclosure» and «Until 1845 the hedge had never been in dispute.»: the hedge was kept under a settled division of work and had never been in dispute, and «both sides agree the thorn was last laid in 1839» puts the last laying six years back, a normal interval.

C “The surveyor came to the bank after the attorneys had begun to write” — refuted by «The previous October a surveyor had chained and pegged the line along the bank, from the ash to the culvert.» against «In November 1845 Ephraim Ruddiforth’s attorney claimed the bank, the ditch and the timber from the stone gap down to the lane.»: the pegging is the October before the November 1845 claim, so it precedes the letters.
justification: Key D follows from matching the two extents through the named landmarks: the claim runs «In November 1845 Ephraim Ruddiforth’s attorney claimed the bank, the ditch and the timber from the stone gap down to the lane.» and the survey runs the same ground, «The previous October a surveyor had chained and pegged the line along the bank, from the ash to the culvert.», with «An ash grew in the stone gap; a culvert ran under the lane.» identifying the ash with the stone gap and the culvert with the lane.
